section_title: How can persecution become an opportunity to bear witness?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 12 But before all this, they will seize you and persecute you. On account of My name they will deliver you to the synagogues and prisons, and they will bring you before kings and governors. 13 This will be your opportunity to serve as witnesses. 14 So make up your mind not to worry beforehand how to defend yourselves. 15 For I will give you speech and wisdom that none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict.

16 You will be betrayed even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you will be put to death. 17 And you will be hated by everyone because of My name. 18 Yet not even a hair of your head will perish. 19 By your patient endurance you will gain your souls.

context_lines: Jesus now says that before these things, His followers will be seized, brought before religious authorities and imprisoned, and made to appear before kings and governors because of His name. He describes these experiences as opportunities to bear witness.

He tells them not to worry beforehand about their defense and promises to give them speech and wisdom their opponents cannot withstand. This instruction concerns their response when brought before hostile authorities.

The warning reaches close to home: relatives and friends will betray them, they will face hatred, and some will be killed. Alongside that warning, Jesus promises that not even a hair will perish and calls them to patient endurance. The promise must be heard together with His explicit warning that some will die.
common_interpretation_lines: Christian readings commonly see a call to enduring trust in God through suffering, with Christ’s help for the testimony His followers must give. Wesley relates the promise about their hair to God’s care and reward, while Calvin describes entrusting one’s life to God even while facing death. These readings keep the promise together with the warning of martyrdom. ([Wesley on Luke 21:18–19](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-luke/); [Calvin on Luke 21:19](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/luke/21.htm))
god_plan_lines: Acts gives concrete examples of the promised witness. Peter speaks before rulers while filled with the Holy Spirit, and Stephen’s opponents cannot withstand the wisdom and Spirit with which he speaks. Stephen is nevertheless killed, praying that Jesus will receive his spirit. God’s help in bearing witness and the reality of suffering appear together in Luke’s continuing account. ([Acts 4:8–13](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/4.htm); [Acts 6:8–12](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/6.htm); [Acts 7:54–60](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/7.htm))

Paul later stands before Agrippa and testifies to the suffering and resurrection of Christ and the light reaching Israel and the Gentiles. He wants those hearing him to share his faith. The forced appearance before rulers becomes an occasion for the saving message to reach people who might otherwise never have heard that witness. ([Acts 26:19–29](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/26.htm))
